SK2200 The field initializer is overwritten by every constructor

A private instance field is given a value at its declaration and every constructor that runs field initializers assigns it again before anything reads it, so the declared value never survives an allocation.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeCompilation
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileno — it reads the whole compilation
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

The initializer is dead work on every allocation, and that is the smaller half. The larger half is that two values are written down for one field and only one of them is ever true, so a reader who looks at the declaration to learn the default learns a value the program never holds. ⚠ Which of the two was meant is a real question and the finding does not answer it. What it asserts is narrower and checkable: the value at the declaration is unreachable. Deleting it is the edit that makes the code say what it does; keeping it and deleting the constructor's assignment is the other repair, and only the author knows which.

Example

Instead of:

sealed class Session {
    readonly int retries = 5;   // never survives a single allocation

    public Session(int given) => retries = given;
}

Write:

sealed class Session {
    readonly int retries;

    public Session(int given) => retries = given;
}

When it does not fire

⚠ Only a constructor that actually runs field initializers counts. C# runs them in constructors that do not chain to this(…), so a chaining constructor is evidence of nothing and is skipped; the rule fires only when every non-chaining constructor overwrites the field. A type with no explicitly declared instance constructor is never examined, because the implicit one writes nothing at all. ⚠ A record, a primary constructor and any constructor Roslyn declared implicitly stop the walk for the whole type, because a record's copy constructor does not run field initializers and a primary constructor's assignments are not constructor statements the walk can read — in both the shape of the evidence is different from the shape the rule checks. ⚠ The write has to be the first thing that touches the field, and nothing before it may run code (#431). It must be a plain x = … or this.x = … at the top level of the constructor body; every statement before it, and the value it writes, must run no code but the language's own — locals, fields, storage properties and built-in operators — and must not touch the field. A getter, a call, an allocation or a user-defined operator can each read the initialized value without naming the field: var s = P; f = 1; with int P => f; measured 71 → 1, and f = Twice(); with Twice() => f * 2 measured 6 → 0. ⚠ Field initializers run *before* the base constructor call, so every base constructor body up to `object`'s is inside the window too, and each one must run no code either. A base constructor that calls an override which reaches the field through a private helper, or tests this for an interface and calls it, reads the initialized value — both measured 5 → 0 — and neither names the field in an override, which is all the old guard looked for. A base class from metadata (Exception, a WinForms Control) cannot be read and declines. This needs every constructor in the compilation, so the rule decides at the end of the compilation and its scope is Compilation. ⚠ A construction that throws inside the window is a reader as well. The initialized value outlives the exception: a finalizer reads it, and so does whoever holds a this the window stored — both measured 5 → 0. So when either is possible — a destructor up the chain, a class that is not sealed and could gain one, or this used as a value in the window — nothing in the window may throw: no other instance initializer, constructor-initializer argument, base body, statement before the write or written value. A sealed type with no finalizer that stores this nowhere may still throw before the write, because nothing is left to see it. ⚠ The initializer itself must be side-effect free, because the fix deletes it: literals, default, nameof, typeof, sizeof, a chain of names, a cast, a unary operator and parentheses over those. = new List<int>() is declined — an allocation whose constructor registers something is exactly what SK2013 and CA1806 argue about, and this rule will not delete a new on its own authority. Private instance fields only; const, static and non-private fields are out of scope, and an auto-property initializer with the same defect is an under-report this rule documents rather than covers. A span carrying a comment or a preprocessor directive is not reported at all, rather than reported without the fix the catalogue promises. Generated code is excluded. ⚠ #423: the initializer must be free to skip — it runs no code and cannot throw. The syntactic test admitted Counter.Next as a name path and (W)4 as a cast, and the audit measured both running before the fix and not after; a division by a value that may be zero is declined for the same reason. ⚠ #431: with every reader above guarded, the fix is safe again. Each measured shape is an executable fixture that goes red when its guard is removed.
